new_quiz.q: What is coupling between two actors?
choices: How far apart the two actors are in the level
How much one actor depends on the other
How many components the two actors share
How often the two actors are saved
new_quiz.explain: Coupling is how much one actor must know about the other. The more it must know, the harder both are to change later.

new_quiz.q: What is a direct reference?
choices: A variable that points to one known actor, so you can call it
A signal that any actor can listen to
A list of functions without any logic
A copy of another Blueprint
new_quiz.explain: A direct reference is a variable of a known type, here BP_Lamp. The button picks one lamp in the level and calls a function on it.

new_quiz.q: What is a Blueprint Interface?
choices: A widget that is drawn on the screen
A variable that stores a location
A window where you edit keyboard shortcuts
A shared list of functions that any actor can answer
new_quiz.explain: An interface only names functions, such as Activate. Any Blueprint that implements it decides for itself what the function does.

new_quiz.q: What is an Event Dispatcher?
choices: A node that waits for some time
A function that returns a value
A signal that other actors can listen to
A volume that fires overlap events
new_quiz.explain: An Event Dispatcher sends out a signal when you call it. Every actor that is bound to it reacts.

new_quiz.q: In the direct reference version, what must the button know about its target?
choices: Nothing at all
Its exact class, BP_Lamp
Only that it is an Actor
Only its position in the level
new_quiz.explain: The variable on the button is of the type BP_Lamp. The button only works with lamps, which is the strongest coupling of the three ways.

new_quiz.q: In the interface version, on which kind of reference does the button call Activate (Message)?
choices: On a plain Actor reference
On a BP_Lamp reference
On a Point Light reference
On a GameMode reference
new_quiz.explain: The message can be sent to any Actor. The button does not need to know the class, and any actor that implements the interface answers.

new_quiz.q: In the Event Dispatcher version, how does the lamp react to the button?
choices: It reads the button on every frame
It calls Activate (Message) on the button
It casts the player to BP_Button
It uses Bind Event to OnPressed
new_quiz.explain: The lamp binds one of its events to OnPressed. When the button calls the dispatcher, the bound event runs.

new_quiz.q: In the Event Dispatcher version, what does the button know about the lamp?
choices: It knows the class of the lamp
It knows the light color of the lamp
It knows nothing about who listens
It knows every function of the lamp
new_quiz.explain: The button only calls OnPressed. The listeners bind themselves, so you can add or remove lamps and never change the button.

new_quiz.q: What is a HUD?
choices: A level that is used only for menus
A camera that follows the player
The information drawn on top of the game, such as the score
The list of actors in the Outliner
new_quiz.explain: HUD is the name for the information shown over the game picture. A score counter is a typical part of it.

new_quiz.q: What is a Widget Blueprint?
choices: An asset that holds text, images and other interface parts
An actor that you place in the level
A file that stores a set of values
A node that prints text to the log
new_quiz.explain: A Widget Blueprint is where you build interface elements. WBP_Score holds a Text widget for the score.

new_quiz.q: Which two nodes put WBP_Score on the screen?
choices: Spawn Actor from Class, then Possess
Create Widget, then Add to Viewport
Get Game State, then Print String
Bind Event, then Remove from Parent
new_quiz.explain: Create Widget makes the widget from the class WBP_Score. Add to Viewport shows it on the screen.

new_quiz.q: On which event of the character do you create the score widget?
choices: Event Tick
Event AnyDamage
Event End Overlap
Event BeginPlay
new_quiz.explain: BeginPlay runs once when the game starts. That is the right moment to create the widget one time.

new_quiz.q: Why should you not update the score text on Tick?
choices: Tick does not run while the game is playing
Tick cannot read variables
Tick runs every frame, so the work is done again and again for no reason
Tick only works in the Level Blueprint
new_quiz.explain: The score changes only now and then. Setting the text every frame repeats the same work with the same result.

new_quiz.q: What is the Event Dispatcher OnScoreChanged in the GameState for?
choices: It tells listeners that the score has changed
It adds 1 to the score every second
It saves the score to disk
It resets the score when the level starts
new_quiz.explain: The GameState calls OnScoreChanged every time the score changes. The widget listens and updates its text only then.

new_quiz.q: Where does WBP_Score start to listen to OnScoreChanged?
choices: On Event Tick of the character
On Event Construct, with Bind Event on the GameState
In the Class Defaults of the GameMode
In the World Settings of the level
new_quiz.explain: Event Construct runs when the widget is created. There the widget gets the GameState, casts it to your class and binds to the dispatcher.

new_quiz.q: You press the test key and the score variable goes up, but the text on the screen stays the same. What do you check first?
choices: That the Text widget uses a large font
That the level has a Player Start
That the widget was added to the viewport two times
That the GameState calls OnScoreChanged after it changes the score
new_quiz.explain: The widget only updates when the dispatcher is called. If the GameState changes the score and does not call OnScoreChanged, the widget never hears about it.

new_quiz.q: What is a kill volume?
choices: An invisible area that ends the try of the player when they touch it
A volume that makes sounds louder
A visible wall that blocks the player
A place where the game remembers progress
new_quiz.explain: A kill volume marks a place where the player fails, for example a pit under the level. Touching it ends the try.

new_quiz.q: What does respawn logic do?
choices: It removes the player from the game for ever
It loads the main menu
It puts the player back in the level after they fail
It saves the level to disk
new_quiz.explain: To respawn means to appear again. The logic decides where and how the player comes back after a failure.

new_quiz.q: Where do you place the kill volume in this quest?
choices: Above the level, in the sky
Below the floor, as a large Box Collision
Around the Player Start
Inside the checkpoint
new_quiz.explain: The volume lies under the level. A player who falls off the floor overlaps the large box and is sent back.

new_quiz.q: Where do you store the last checkpoint?
choices: In a text file in the project folder
In the name of the checkpoint actor
In the material of the floor
In a Transform variable that the GameMode can read
new_quiz.explain: A Transform variable such as LastCheckpoint in the GameMode or the GameState holds the respawn place. The GameMode reads it when it moves the player back.

new_quiz.q: What does the checkpoint Blueprint do when the player overlaps it?
choices: It destroys the player
It writes its own transform into the LastCheckpoint variable
It moves itself to the player
It restarts the level
new_quiz.explain: The checkpoint saves where it stands. From then on, a respawn brings the player to this place.

new_quiz.q: Which node moves the player back to the checkpoint?
choices: Set Actor Transform
Destroy Actor
Add to Viewport
Play Sound at Location
new_quiz.explain: An event on the GameMode calls Set Actor Transform on the player with the stored transform. The player is moved, not destroyed.

new_quiz.q: How do you make a level use your new GameMode Blueprint?
choices: Drag the GameMode into the viewport
Add the GameMode to the kill volume
Set it as the GameMode Override in World Settings
Name the level after the GameMode
new_quiz.explain: GameMode Override in World Settings chooses the GameMode for that level. Your respawn event only exists when the level runs your GameMode.

new_quiz.q: Why do you make your GameMode a child of the GameMode of the template?
choices: A child Blueprint cannot be changed by mistake
A child Blueprint runs faster than its parent
A child Blueprint needs no World Settings
A child Blueprint keeps the settings of the template, such as the character
new_quiz.explain: A child Blueprint inherits everything from its parent. You still play as the template character and only add the new event and variable.

new_quiz.q: What is a game loop in this quest?
choices: A Timeline that plays without end
The event that runs on every frame
The full circle of play, from the action of the player to the win
A level that loads itself again and again
new_quiz.explain: The loop joins action, counting and winning. Building all of it proves that the separate pieces work together.

new_quiz.q: What is a Blueprint Interface?
choices: A widget that shows the score
A list of functions that different Blueprints can share
A file that stores the values of a pickup
A window where you package the game
new_quiz.explain: The interface names functions such as Interact. The character calls the function on the pickup and does not need to know the class of the pickup.

new_quiz.q: Where does the pickup Blueprint get its name and point value from?
choices: From a Data Asset
From values typed into the graph
From the Output Log
From the World Settings
new_quiz.explain: The values are stored in Data Asset instances made from a Primary Data Asset class. You can change them without editing the graph.

new_quiz.q: Which two Blueprints share the work of score and win?
choices: The pickup keeps the score, and the character declares the win
The Level Blueprint keeps the score, and the widget declares the win
The character keeps the score, and the pickup declares the win
The GameState keeps the score, and the GameMode declares the win
new_quiz.explain: Shared information such as the score belongs in the GameState. The rule that decides the win belongs in the GameMode.

new_quiz.q: How does the player interact with at least one pickup type?
choices: Through a console command
Through an Enhanced Input action named IA_Interact
Through a click on the Outliner
Through a show flag of the viewport
new_quiz.explain: You create the Input Action IA_Interact, add it to the Input Mapping Context of the template with a key, and handle it on the character.

new_quiz.q: What do you add for every actor reference that you use?
choices: A Delay node and a Timeline
A second copy of the reference
An Is Valid check and a log warning
A Text Render actor
new_quiz.explain: The Is Valid check stops the graph from using an empty reference. The warning in the log tells you where the problem is.

new_quiz.q: What does it mean to package the project?
choices: To build a version of the game that runs outside the editor
To compress the Content folder into a ZIP file
To save all levels at the same time
To send the project to another learner
new_quiz.explain: Packaging builds a version of the game that runs without the editor. A development build is such a version made for testing.

new_quiz.q: Where do you start packaging in the editor?
choices: In the Trace menu at the bottom of the editor window
In the three dots menu next to the Play button
In Edit, then Editor Preferences
In the Platforms button in the main toolbar, then your platform, then Package Project
new_quiz.explain: The Platforms button lists the platforms you can build for. You choose your platform and then Package Project.

new_quiz.q: What is a master material?
choices: A material that can only be used on one mesh
A material that is locked and cannot be opened
A material that the engine creates for every project
One material built with parameters, from which you make instances
new_quiz.explain: A master material leaves some values open as parameters. Many instances can then reuse the same graph with different values.

new_quiz.q: What is a parameter in a material?
choices: A value, such as a color, that you leave open to change
A texture that is imported from a file
A comment that explains the graph
A mesh that the material is applied to
new_quiz.explain: A parameter is a named value in the graph. Instances of the material can set it to their own value.

new_quiz.q: What is a Material Instance?
choices: A full copy of the material graph that you edit node by node
A light copy of a material that only changes its parameters
A screenshot of a material
A material that has no parent
new_quiz.explain: A Material Instance has no graph of its own. It uses the graph of its parent and only sets the parameters.

new_quiz.q: Which kind of parameter do you use for BaseColor?
choices: A Scalar parameter
A Texture parameter
A Vector parameter
A Boolean parameter
new_quiz.explain: A color has several channels, so it needs a Vector parameter. Roughness, Metallic and EmissiveStrength are single numbers, so they are Scalar parameters.

new_quiz.q: How do you build the glow of the master material?
choices: Connect Roughness to the Emissive input
Multiply EmissiveStrength by the color and connect the result to the Emissive input
Add Metallic to the color and connect the result to Base Color
Connect EmissiveStrength to the Roughness input
new_quiz.explain: The color gives the glow its tint and EmissiveStrength sets how strong it is. With the value at 0, the material does not glow.

new_quiz.q: Why do you give every parameter a Group?
choices: Groups keep the parameter list tidy when you open an instance
Groups make the material render faster
Groups are needed before the material can be saved
Groups lock the parameters against changes
new_quiz.explain: In a Material Instance, the parameters are listed by group. Good groups make the right value easy to find.

new_quiz.q: What should the three instances tell the player?
choices: How many materials the level uses
Which object was placed first
How large each object is
The role of each object, by its color
new_quiz.explain: One instance marks things the player can use, one marks hazards, and one marks scenery. The player learns the rule from the colors.

new_quiz.q: You need a fourth look, for example blue for a goal object. What is the right way to add it?
choices: Copy the whole master material and change its nodes
Paint the mesh blue in another program
Make another Material Instance from the master and change its parameters
Add a second Emissive input to the master material
new_quiz.explain: That is what the master material is for. A new instance only needs new parameter values, and the graph is not touched.
